Topic: E.003 COSO Principle 10 -- preventive detective control design
MicroTopic: COSO Principle 10 -- preventive detective control design
Stem: Crestline Distribution, a regional wholesale distributor of building materials with $180 million in annual revenue, experienced a 340% increase in inventory shrinkage over three consecutive quarters. Controller Elena Vasquez reviewed the control portfolio and noted that Crestline performs weekly cycle counts of all high-value inventory items, reconciles the perpetual inventory system to the general ledger monthly within 72 hours of month-end, and investigates all variances exceeding 2% of book value. Despite these controls, it was discovered that a warehouse supervisor had been removing inventory after hours and selling it through an unauthorized online marketplace over an 11-month period. The warehouse entrance had no access card reader or biometric scanner -- employees simply signed a paper log that was not reviewed by any supervisor. Elena concluded that the control breakdown was caused by over-reliance on detective controls without adequate preventive controls. Which of the following statements best supports her conclusion?

Choices.A: The weekly cycle counts identified shrinkage variances each quarter, but the variances were within the 2% investigation threshold and therefore were not escalated to management for further inquiry.
Choices.B: The monthly general ledger reconciliation consistently identified the inventory-to-book discrepancies within the 72-hour window, confirming that the detective controls functioned as designed throughout the period.
Choices.C: The warehouse entrance lacked physical access controls -- no badge reader, no biometric scanner, no turnstile -- meaning unauthorized removal could occur without any barrier, and the cycle counts could only identify the loss after inventory had already been removed from the premises.
Choices.D: The warehouse supervisor had authorization to approve inventory adjustments up to $5,000 without secondary approval, which allowed small quantities of missing inventory to be written off incrementally without triggering management review.

ExplanationCorrect: COSO Principle 10 requires that an organization select and develop control activities that contribute to the mitigation of risks to the achievement of objectives to acceptable levels. Preventive controls are designed to deter errors or irregularities from occurring, while detective controls identify errors or irregularities after they have already occurred. In this scenario, Crestline's control portfolio was dominated by detective controls: cycle counts, reconciliations, and variance analysis all identify shrinkage only after inventory has been removed. The absence of a preventive physical access control at the warehouse entrance -- no badge reader, no biometric scanner, no turnstile -- meant that unauthorized removal could occur without any barrier whatsoever. Option C correctly identifies that the lack of physical access controls at the point of entry meant there was no preventive control to stop the unauthorized removal before it happened. The cycle counts functioned properly as detective controls, but by the time they identified the loss, the inventory was already gone and sold. A balanced control portfolio requires both preventive and detective controls; relying exclusively on detective controls to protect physical assets creates an unacceptable window of exposure between the occurrence of a loss event and its detection. The business interpretation is that management must assess whether each significant risk has both preventive and detective controls, and that a control environment heavy on reconciliation and light on physical security creates vulnerability to asset misappropriation regardless of how frequently detective controls operate.

ExplanationWrongA: Option A identifies a correct observation -- that the cycle counts detected variances within the investigation threshold -- but misinterprets the conclusion. The fact that the variances were within the 2% threshold does not explain the root cause of the control breakdown. The shrinkage occurred because there was no preventive control to stop the warehouse supervisor from removing inventory in the first place. Even if the threshold had been lower and the variances had been escalated, the inventory would still have been removed before detection. The issue is not the sensitivity of detective controls but the absence of preventive controls at the point of access. A candidate selecting this option may be focusing on detective control thresholds rather than on the fundamental distinction between controls that prevent events from occurring and controls that detect events after the fact.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B describes controls that functioned correctly -- the reconciliation process identified discrepancies within the stated service-level window. However, this actually undermines rather than supports Elena's conclusion. If the detective controls were working as designed and still could not prevent the $47,000 loss, then the root cause is indeed the absence of preventive controls. Selecting this option suggests the candidate is evaluating control effectiveness without distinguishing between controls that detect after the fact and controls that prevent before the fact. The reconciliation working correctly is evidence that detective controls alone are not sufficient by themselves to protect physical assets.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D identifies a legitimate concern about authorization limits, but it misidentifies the root cause. The warehouse supervisor's ability to approve small write-offs without secondary approval is an authorization control issue, not the reason the inventory was removed without detection in the first place. Even without that authorization, the supervisor could still have removed the inventory -- the missing preventive control at the warehouse entrance was the primary gap that enabled the fraud. A candidate selecting this option may be confusing an authorization deficiency with a physical access control deficiency. While both are control activities under COSO Principle 10, the scenario facts point specifically to the absence of physical access barriers as the enabling condition for the unauthorized removal.

Topic: E.009 COSO Principle 15 -- SOC report evaluation
Stem: Northpoint Manufacturing, a mid-sized industrial equipment producer with 1,800 employees, outsources payroll processing to PayCorp Services, a third-party service organization. PayCorp issues a SOC 1 Type 2 report annually, which Northpoint's CFO David Chen reviews as part of the company's internal control over financial reporting assessment. The 2026 SOC 1 Type 2 report contains an unmodified opinion on the suitability of design and operating effectiveness of PayCorp's controls. However, in the section titled 'Complementary User Entity Controls,' the report states that the user entity is responsible for: (a) reviewing and approving all payroll register changes before each processing cycle, and (b) verifying that terminated employees are removed from the payroll master file within one business day of termination. David discovers that Northpoint has not been performing the pre-processing payroll register review for the past eight months -- the HR manager had been approving payroll registers after processing instead of before. No incorrect payments have been identified during this period, and the after-processing review caught three minor data entry errors that were corrected before the next pay cycle. David must evaluate whether this represents a deficiency in Northpoint's internal control over financial reporting and determine the appropriate response. Which of the following is the most accurate assessment?

Choices.A: This is not a control deficiency because PayCorp received an unmodified SOC 1 Type 2 opinion, confirming that the service organization's controls are suitably designed and operating effectively, and Northpoint can rely on that opinion for its own internal control assessment.
Choices.B: This is a control deficiency because the SOC 1 Type 2 report identified a complementary user entity control that Northpoint was required to implement as a condition of the service organization's control environment, and the company deviated from the prescribed control for eight months.
Choices.C: This is not a control deficiency because no incorrect payments resulted from the deviation, the after-processing review provided a compensating detective control that caught errors before the next pay cycle, and the deviation did not affect the fair presentation of the financial statements.
Choices.D: This is a material weakness because the failure to perform the pre-processing review for eight months creates a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement in Northpoint's financial statements would not be prevented or detected on a timely basis by the company's internal controls.

ExplanationCorrect: COSO Principle 15 requires that the organization communicates with external parties regarding matters affecting the functioning of internal control. When an organization outsources a business process to a service organization, the SOC 1 Type 2 report serves as the primary communication mechanism about the service organization's internal controls. A critical component of the SOC report is the listing of complementary user entity controls -- controls that the user organization must implement for the service organization's control objectives to be achieved. These controls are not optional; they are an integral part of the control environment described in the SOC report. In this scenario, PayCorp's unmodified opinion is explicitly conditioned on Northpoint performing the pre-processing payroll register review. The opinion states that PayCorp's controls were suitably designed and operated effectively assuming that the user entity controls were in place. By not performing this control for eight months, Northpoint has a control deficiency -- a shortcoming in internal control such that the control does not enable management or employees, in the normal course of performing their assigned functions, to prevent or detect misstatements on a timely basis. The fact that no errors resulted does not negate the existence of the deficiency; a control deficiency exists when a necessary control is missing or not operating as designed, regardless of whether a misstatement has actually occurred. Option B correctly identifies the deficiency. The business interpretation is that management must read SOC reports holistically -- an unmodified opinion on the service organization's controls does not relieve the user entity of its responsibility to implement the complementary user entity controls listed in the report. Failing to implement those controls means the overall control objective may not be achieved, even if the service organization performed perfectly.

ExplanationWrongA: Option A reflects a common misunderstanding about SOC reports. An unmodified opinion on a SOC 1 Type 2 report means that the service organization's controls were suitably designed and operated effectively during the review period. However, this opinion is conditioned on the user entity implementing the complementary user entity controls listed in the report. The service auditor cannot opine on controls that are the user entity's responsibility, and the opinion does not cover the user entity's failure to implement required complementary controls. A candidate selecting this option may incorrectly assume that outsourcing transfers all control responsibility to the service organization. In reality, the user entity retains responsibility for the controls designated as complementary user entity controls, and failing to implement them means the overall control objective may not be achieved regardless of the service organization's performance.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C incorrectly applies a 'no harm, no foul' logic that is inconsistent with the COSO internal control framework. A control deficiency is defined by the absence or inadequate design or operation of a control, not by whether a misstatement has actually occurred. The pre-processing review is a preventive control designed to catch payroll errors before payments are made; the after-processing review is a detective control that identifies errors after the fact. While the after-processing review did catch three errors, the preventive control's absence meant there was a period during which errors could have resulted in incorrect payments that the detective control would not catch until after disbursement. A candidate selecting this option may be evaluating control effectiveness by outcome rather than by design and operation.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D overstates the severity of the control deficiency. While the failure to perform the complementary user entity control for eight months is a control deficiency, it does not automatically rise to the level of a material weakness. A material weakness requires a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement of the financial statements would not be prevented or detected on a timely basis. In this scenario, Northpoint had a compensating detective control (after-processing review) that caught errors, and payroll expense for a mid-sized manufacturer is evaluated for materiality against total operating expenses. The after-processing review provided a mitigating control that reduces the likelihood of a material misstatement. A candidate selecting this option may be conflating any control deficiency with a material weakness without evaluating the likelihood and magnitude criteria under the applicable auditing and internal control standards that distinguish the two classifications.

Topic: E.035 COSO ERM -- risk appetite strategic alignment
MicroTopic: COSO ERM risk appetite strategic alignment
Stem: Apex Industrial Corporation, a publicly traded manufacturer of aerospace components with $4.2 billion in annual revenue, operates in 18 countries across North America, Europe, and Asia. The board of directors approved a corporate risk appetite statement three years ago that classifies operational risk appetite as 'Moderate -- the organization accepts operational risks that offer commensurate expected returns and can be managed within existing control frameworks without requiring extraordinary mitigation measures.' The CEO now proposes a $780 million investment to build a new manufacturing campus in a country classified by Apex's ERM function as 'High Geopolitical Risk' due to: (a) two incidents of government expropriation of foreign-owned industrial assets in the past five years, (b) unpredictable changes to foreign ownership regulations that were enacted without notice or transition periods, and (c) a local court system that the company's external legal counsel rates as providing limited recourse for foreign investors. The projected return on invested capital for the project is 18%, compared to Apex's weighted average cost of capital of 9% and the company's historical average new-plant ROI of 14%. The board's risk committee has asked the Chief Risk Officer to evaluate whether this proposal is consistent with the stated risk appetite. Which of the following represents the most supportable governance conclusion?

Choices.A: The proposal is consistent with the stated risk appetite because the 18% projected return exceeds the company's cost of capital by a wide margin and exceeds historical new-plant ROI by 400 basis points, demonstrating that the expected returns are commensurate with the risks undertaken.
Choices.B: The proposal is consistent with the stated risk appetite because operational risk appetite is measured at the plant-operations level, not the strategic-investment level, and the manufacturing processes -- once the facility is operational -- can be managed within standard manufacturing control frameworks such as quality management systems and safety protocols.
Choices.C: The proposal is inconsistent with the stated risk appetite because the $780 million capital outlay exceeds the board's implied single-project concentration threshold, and concentration risk of this magnitude at the enterprise level requires explicit board revision of risk appetite before commitment.
Choices.D: The proposal is inconsistent with the stated risk appetite because the country's geopolitical risk profile -- including government expropriation risk, unpredictable regulatory changes, and limited legal recourse -- represents risks that cannot be managed within Apex's existing control frameworks and therefore exceed the 'Moderate' operational risk tolerance established by the board.

ExplanationCorrect: Under the COSO Enterprise Risk Management framework, risk appetite is the amount of risk, on a broad level, that an organization is willing to accept in pursuit of its value creation objectives. A fundamental principle of COSO ERM is that risk appetite and strategy must be aligned -- the board sets risk appetite as a boundary condition, and management must ensure that strategic decisions fall within that boundary. The key question is whether the proposed investment's risk profile falls within or exceeds the board's stated appetite. In this scenario, the country is classified by Apex's own ERM function as High Geopolitical Risk, characterized by three specific threats that are outside the organization's ability to control or mitigate through standard internal control frameworks: (1) government expropriation of foreign-owned assets -- a sovereign risk that no internal control framework can prevent or recover from; (2) unpredictable regulatory changes -- which create compliance uncertainty that exceeds what existing legal and regulatory monitoring programs can address; and (3) limited legal recourse -- meaning the organization has no effective remedy through local institutions if these risks materialize. The Moderate risk appetite statement explicitly requires that risks be manageable 'within existing control frameworks without requiring extraordinary mitigation measures.' The geopolitical risks in this country fail this criterion -- they would require extraordinary mitigation such as political risk insurance, bilateral investment treaty protections, or sovereign guarantees, none of which are part of Apex's existing control framework. The 18% projected return does not cure this governance problem because risk appetite is a boundary condition, not a cost-benefit tradeoff; returns above the cost of capital do not make a risk that exceeds stated appetite automatically acceptable. Option D correctly identifies that the risk profile exceeds the stated appetite, requiring either rejection of the proposal or explicit board revision of the risk appetite statement. The business interpretation is that risk appetite statements are governance instruments, not aspiration statements. When a proposed strategy's risk profile exceeds the stated appetite, the board must either reject the proposal, revise the risk appetite to accommodate the new strategy, or require additional mitigation that brings the residual risk within the acceptable boundary before proceeding.

ExplanationWrongA: Option A reflects the common fallacy that higher expected financial returns alone justify any level of risk. While COSO ERM recognizes that organizations accept risk in pursuit of returns, the framework requires that the nature and magnitude of risk remain within the stated appetite regardless of the projected return. The 18% ROI exceeds the cost of capital, but this is a purely quantitative analysis that ignores the qualitative dimension of risk appetite -- specifically, whether the risks can be managed within existing frameworks. A candidate selecting this option may be applying a financial evaluation (return exceeds hurdle rate) without considering the governance dimension of risk appetite. The risk appetite statement is a board-level governance control, not a financial optimization tool. Even a 50% projected return would not make a risk that exceeds stated appetite automatically acceptable without board reconsideration of the appetite itself.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B contains two errors. First, operational risk appetite applies to the organization's operational activities as a whole, including strategic decisions about where and how to operate. It is not limited to the manufacturing process level -- the decision to locate operations in a geopolitically unstable region is itself an operational risk decision that must be evaluated against the stated appetite. Second, the assertion that plant operations 'once built' can be managed within standard frameworks ignores the fact that the geopolitical risk exposure continues for the entire life of the investment. The government could expropriate the facility at any time during its 20-to-30-year operating life; standard manufacturing controls such as quality management and safety protocols provide no protection against sovereign risk. A candidate selecting this option may be artificially segmenting strategic risk from operational risk in a way that is inconsistent with COSO ERM's enterprise-wide view of risk.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C introduces a fact not present in the scenario -- there is no stated board capital allocation threshold or single-project concentration limit mentioned in the risk appetite statement or scenario facts. The question asks the candidate to evaluate the proposal against the stated risk appetite, not against hypothetical concentration risk policies. While $780 million is a substantial investment for a $4.2 billion company, the governance issue is not the dollar amount but the nature of the operational risks being accepted relative to the stated appetite. A candidate selecting this option may be substituting quantitative threshold analysis (the investment is 'too big') for the qualitative risk appetite analysis that the question requires. COSO ERM requires evaluation of whether the risk profile is consistent with stated tolerances, not whether the investment size exceeds an arbitrary ceiling.

Topic: E.038 COSO Principle 11 -- IT general controls access migration
MicroTopic: COSO Principle 11 -- IT general controls access migration
Stem: Meridian Healthcare Solutions, a regional healthcare services provider with 4,200 employees, completed a migration from a legacy on-premise ERP system to a cloud-based ERP platform in January 2026. Six months after go-live, an internal audit identified that 23% of user accounts (966 of 4,200) retained access permissions from the legacy system that conflict with their new role-based access assignments in the cloud ERP. Specifically, 312 accounts in the accounts payable department retained general ledger posting access that was appropriate in the legacy system but was explicitly removed from the AP role in the new system's security design. An additional 198 accounts had purchase order approval limits in the new system that exceeded their legacy-system limits by an average of 340%, with no corresponding change in job responsibilities or documented business justification. The migration project plan required that all user access be re-certified by department heads before go-live, but the certification was completed for only 61% of departments. The remaining 39% went live with legacy permissions mapped automatically by a conversion script. Which IT general control area most directly failed, and what is the primary remediation required?

Choices.A: Access control -- the legacy-to-cloud role mapping process failed to ensure that permissions in the new system were restricted to those necessary for each user's current job responsibilities. The primary remediation requires an enterprise-wide access recertification for all 4,200 accounts and implementation of periodic user access reviews.
Choices.B: Change management -- the ERP migration was implemented without adequate end-to-end testing of the role-mapping conversion scripts, allowing legacy permissions to propagate into the production environment. The primary remediation requires re-executing the role-mapping migration with corrected conversion scripts in a controlled change window.
Choices.C: Segregation of duties -- the 312 AP accounts with general ledger posting access represent an incompatible function combination that creates material fraud risk. The primary remediation requires immediate revocation of GL posting access from all AP department users, followed by a segregation-of-duties conflict analysis across all departments.
Choices.D: System operations -- the cloud ERP vendor failed to properly configure the role-based access controls during the implementation phase that were specified in the statement of work. The primary remediation requires the vendor to perform a root cause analysis and implement corrective configuration changes under the service level agreement.

ExplanationCorrect: COSO Principle 11 requires that the organization select and develop general control activities over technology to support the achievement of objectives. IT general controls (ITGCs) encompass access security, change management, system operations, and program development controls. Access control is the ITGC domain that governs how users are granted, modified, and revoked access to information systems. The principle of least privilege -- that users should have only the access necessary to perform their assigned job responsibilities -- is a foundational access control concept. Three facts in this scenario point to an access control failure rather than a change management or segregation-of-duties failure: (1) the cloud ERP migration involved a deliberate role redesign where AP users were explicitly not supposed to have GL posting access, yet 312 accounts retained it, indicating the role-to-permission mapping was never validated against the new security design; (2) purchase order approval limits increased by an average of 340% without business justification, indicating that permissions were not calibrated to actual job responsibilities; and (3) the department head recertification -- which is an access control activity, not a change management control -- was completed for only 61% of departments, meaning 39% of users went live with unverified access. The root cause is that the access provisioning process failed to ensure that permissions granted in the new system were appropriate, authorized, and aligned with job responsibilities. Remediation must address the access control lifecycle: an immediate enterprise-wide recertification to correct the current state, and implementation of periodic user access reviews to prevent recurrence. Option A correctly identifies the ITGC domain and the proportionate remediation. The business interpretation is that technology migrations create concentrated access control risk because role definitions, permission models, and user populations shift simultaneously. A rigorous access recertification process both before and after migration is essential to maintaining the principle of least privilege and ensuring that no user carries forward permissions that are no longer appropriate.

While the ERP migration was a significant change, the specific failure identified -- retained legacy permissions and inflated approval limits -- is an access provisioning issue, not a change testing defect. Additionally, re-executing the entire role-mapping migration would be operationally disruptive and disproportionate when the same outcome can be achieved through access recertification in the live production environment. Remediation focused exclusively on revoking GL access from AP users would leave the 654 other accounts with inappropriate permissions unaddressed -- including the 198 accounts with unjustified purchase order approval limit increases. Furthermore, segregation of duties is a control objective, not a control activity; access controls (including role design, permission assignment, and periodic recertification) are the mechanisms that enforce segregation of duties. A candidate selecting this option may be correctly identifying a specific control weakness but failing to recognize that it is one manifestation of a systemic access management breakdown requiring enterprise-wide remediation rather than a targeted revocation.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D incorrectly assigns responsibility for the access control failure to the cloud ERP vendor. Under the shared responsibility model that governs cloud computing, the vendor is responsible for the security OF the cloud (infrastructure security, platform security, physical security), but the customer is responsible for security IN the cloud -- including user access management, role configuration, permission assignment, and access recertification. The 23% permission conflict rate, the incomplete department head recertification, and the purchase order approval limit escalation are all customer-side access management failures that fall squarely within Meridian's responsibility. A candidate selecting this option may misunderstand the shared responsibility model, incorrectly assuming that the cloud vendor bears responsibility for all control failures in a cloud environment. The remediation must be performed by Meridian, not the vendor, because access provisioning, role design, and user recertification are customer responsibilities under any cloud service model.

Topic: E.069 COSO Principle 10 -- segregation duties small entity
MicroTopic: COSO Principle 10 -- segregation duties small entity
Stem: Hope Community Foundation is a nonprofit organization with $3.2 million in annual contributions, a staff of 12, and an accounting department of 4 people. Due to limited staffing, the same accounting clerk, Maria, performs the following duties: (1) opens all incoming mail containing donor checks, (2) prepares the daily bank deposit and delivers it to the bank, (3) records all cash receipts in the general ledger, and (4) performs the monthly bank reconciliation. The board of directors, aware of the segregation of duties concern, has implemented the following compensating controls: the executive director reviews the bank reconciliation monthly and initials it; the board treasurer receives the unopened monthly bank statement directly at home and reviews it before forwarding to Maria for reconciliation; and an independent external auditor performs surprise cash counts twice per year. During the most recent audit, the external auditor identified that Maria had been recording fictitious donor-restricted contributions at the beginning of each month, then reclassifying them to unrestricted revenue when the 'donor' predictably failed to send payment. Over 14 months, this scheme enabled Maria to skim $47,000 in cash from donor checks before they were deposited, and the fictitious contribution entries in the general ledger masked the shortfall. The executive director had initialed all 14 monthly bank reconciliations without noting any irregularities. Which compensating control gap most directly enabled the fraud to remain undetected for 14 months?

Choices.A: The board treasurer's receipt of the bank statement before forwarding it to Maria -- the treasurer should have performed the bank reconciliation personally rather than forwarding the statement to the same person who handles cash receipts and general ledger recording.
Choices.B: The executive director's review of the bank reconciliation -- the executive director initialed the reconciliations each month but did not compare the reconciliation to the general ledger detail or trace reconciling items to supporting documentation, rendering the review a perfunctory rather than a substantive control.
Choices.C: The concentration of cash receipts recording and bank reconciliation in Maria's hands -- regardless of the compensating controls, no single person should both record cash receipts and perform the bank reconciliation, because the reconciliation cannot serve as an independent check when prepared by the same person who recorded the transactions being reconciled.
Choices.D: The external auditor's surprise cash counts -- performing surprise counts only twice per year provided insufficient coverage for an entity with a known segregation-of-duties weakness, and the auditor should have been conducting monthly surprise procedures given the elevated fraud risk.

ExplanationCorrect: COSO Principle 10 requires that the organization select and develop control activities that contribute to the mitigation of risks to the achievement of objectives to acceptable levels. In a small entity, absolute segregation of duties may not be achievable due to limited personnel, but management must implement compensating controls that provide an equivalent level of mitigation. The most fundamental incompatible function combination in the cash receipts cycle is the combination of recording transactions and performing the reconciliation intended to verify those transactions. When the same person records cash receipts and performs the bank reconciliation, the reconciliation ceases to function as a detective control -- it becomes a self-review activity. COSO explicitly identifies this as an incompatible function combination that should be segregated wherever possible, and when segregation is not possible, compensating controls must provide truly independent verification. In this scenario, the board implemented three compensating controls, but all of them failed because none addressed the root incompatibility: Maria controlled both sides of the reconciliation equation. She could record fictitious contributions in the general ledger, not deposit the corresponding checks (because they were skimmed), and then reconcile the bank statement to her own fictitious general ledger entries. The treasurer receiving the bank statement first did not prevent this because Maria still performed the reconciliation. The executive director's review was ineffective because Maria controlled the underlying data that the reconciliation was built upon. Option C correctly identifies that the concentration of cash receipts recording and bank reconciliation in a single person is the root incompatibility that served as the enabling condition for the fraud for 14 months. The business interpretation for small entities is that certain incompatible functions are so fundamental that compensating controls must involve transferring one of the functions to a different person, not merely adding layers of supervisory review on top of the existing incompatible assignment. The board should have assigned the bank reconciliation to the executive director, the board treasurer, or another staff member who does not handle cash receipts or record them in the general ledger.

ExplanationWrongA: Option A correctly identifies that the treasurer's role in the compensating control framework was insufficient, but it misidentifies the remedy relative to the root cause. Requiring the treasurer to perform the bank reconciliation personally would indeed address the incompatibility, but this represents the same fundamental issue that Option C identifies: the bank reconciliation must be performed by someone other than the person who records cash receipts. The question asks what most directly enabled the fraud to go undetected -- the enabling condition was the structural concentration of incompatible functions in Maria, not the insufficiency of any one specific compensating control. A candidate selecting this option may be correctly analyzing the compensating control weakness but stopping at the control level rather than tracing the failure back to the root incompatibility that made all layered compensating controls unreliable.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B identifies a genuine weakness in the executive director's review -- initialing the bank reconciliation without comparing it to the general ledger detail or tracing reconciling items to source documents rendered the review perfunctory. However, even a thorough, substantive review by the executive director would have been undermined by the same fundamental problem: Maria controlled both the cash receipts records and the bank reconciliation, so she could manipulate the reconciliation to appear to balance regardless of the executive director's scrutiny. The executive director would have been reviewing a reconciliation built from data that Maria had the ability to manipulate on both the cash receipts side (fictitious entries) and the reconciliation side (matching to her own entries in the general ledger). A candidate selecting this option may be focusing on the surface-level failure of a specific control execution (the review was not deep enough) rather than recognizing that the structural incompatibility rendered any review-based compensating control inherently unreliable as long as the same person controlled both the source data and the reconciliation.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D misidentifies both the nature and the responsibility of the compensating control. The external auditor's surprise cash counts are external corroborative audit procedures, not management compensating controls. Under COSO Principle 10, compensating controls are management's responsibility and must operate continuously as an integral part of the entity's internal control system -- not periodically as an external audit procedure. Even if the auditor had conducted monthly surprise counts, this would not address the root incompatibility that enabled the fraud to occur on a daily basis between audit visits. A candidate selecting this option may be confusing external audit procedures with internal compensating controls under the COSO framework. The external auditor is not part of the entity's internal control system; compensating controls must be designed, implemented, and operated by management as part of the ongoing control environment.
